factual_claims.claim: Approximately 70% of highly AI-exposed workers (26.5 million out of 37.1 million) have above-median adaptive capacity to manage job transitions.
Approximately 6.1 million workers, primarily in clerical and administrative roles, face high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity.
86% of workers with high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity are women.
Highly AI-exposed occupations with low adaptive capacity are geographically concentrated in college towns and state capitals, particularly in the Mountain West and Midwest.

unmapped_concepts.reason: The concept of 'adaptive capacity' as a counterweight to 'exposure' is a fundamental tension in all three POV camps regarding how to manage technological change.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Adaptive capacity is a sign of a dynamic, healthy workforce that can leverage AI to transition into higher-value roles, proving that AI disruption is a manageable transition.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Adaptive capacity is a necessary but insufficient buffer; it doesn't protect against the most catastrophic, irreversible AI failures, and relying on it could lead to complacency.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Adaptive capacity is a measure of worker resilience that policymakers must actively support, as it is currently unevenly distributed and threatened by AI-driven labor market shifts.
